summary.text: The center of mass is the balance point of an object or a group of objects: the one point where the weighted positions of all the mass add up to zero.
It can sit outside the body, as with a horseshoe or a donut, and for separate bodies it may not match any single member.
Pushing a rigid body through it speeds the body up without spinning it, so mechanics calculations are often simpler measured from this point.

facts.label: Statistical analogy
facts.value: The mean location of the mass

facts.label: Center of mass frame
facts.value: The system's center of mass is at rest

items.prompt: A donut has the same density throughout. Where is its balance point?

options.label: Inside the dough, near the edge
At the center, within the hole
On its top surface
It has none, being hollow

items.explain: For uniform density it is at the centroid, and for open shapes like a donut that point can lie outside the material.

items.prompt: You push a rigid crate with a force aimed exactly at its balance point. What does it do?

options.label: It starts spinning without speeding up
It rotates about its heaviest corner
Nothing, since the force cancels
It accelerates straight with no turning

items.explain: A force through the center of mass causes linear acceleration without angular acceleration.

items.prompt: Astronomers find the balance point of all the planets together. Must it lie at one of the planets?

options.label: No, it may match none of them
Yes, at the heaviest planet
Yes, at the planet nearest the middle
Yes, but only if masses are equal

items.explain: For separate bodies such as the Solar System's planets, the center of mass may not correspond to any individual member.

items.prompt: A uniform wooden ruler is balanced on one finger. Where is your finger?

options.label: One third from an end
At the heavier end
At the geometric middle
Anywhere along it

items.explain: Balance point is the center of mass, which for uniform density is the centroid, the middle of the ruler.

items.prompt: Archimedes found that several weights at different spots on a lever give the same torque as if gathered at one point. Which point?

options.label: The fulcrum
The center of mass
The heaviest weight's spot
The end of the lever

items.explain: He showed the torque equals what it would be if all the weights were moved to their center of mass.

items.prompt: Why do engineers separate center of mass from center of gravity for a satellite near a planet?

options.label: Gravity varies across it and can twist it
A satellite has no spread-out mass at all
Gravity does not act on things in orbit
The two always differ by a fixed amount

items.explain: Gravity varies across the satellite, so a horizontal offset between the two points produces a torque.
